div.div: The platform speaks HTTP and nothing else. An agent reachable only through a Python or Java SDK, or over gRPC or SOAP, has no address for it to POST to. A thin FastAPI application with one route gives it one.

div.span: FastAPI or Flask, one POST route

Checks the bearer token, pulls the last user message
out of the messages array, calls the agent the only way
it can be called, and shapes the answer back into JSON.

div.div:
@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(request: ChatRequest, _=Depends(verify_token)):
# {INPUT} lands in the last user message
user_message = next((m.content for m in reversed(request.messages) if m.role == "user"), "")
system_prompt = next((m.content for m in request.messages if m.role == "system"), "")
response = agent_sdk.chat(system=system_prompt, user=user_message)
# OpenAI-shaped, so the response template is a path the customer already knows
return {"choices": [{"message": {"role": "assistant", "content": response.text}, "finish_reason": "stop"}]}

div.b: Anything other than 200 is an error, not a finding

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 648px; height: 1px; padding-top: 787px; margin-left: 19px;

div.div:
The shim has to return HTTP 200 with a JSON body at the mapped
path. A 500 on a prompt the SDK did not like becomes a scan error
and the attack is lost, so catch exceptions inside the route and
return the failure text as content instead of letting it escape.

div.div:
Where there is Kubernetes near the agent, a Custom Target Adapter
does this job with nothing extra to host, and no new internet-facing
service to secure and decommission. Build time here is two to four
hours for a single-method SDK, four to eight once gRPC stubs are in it.
